reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Presents with the features of large bowel obstruction: gross abdominal distension, colicky pain, absolute constipation, and often relatively little vomiting early on
Most common in elderly, institutionalised, or neuropsychiatric patients and those with chronic constipation and a long redundant sigmoid loop on a narrow mesenteric base
The abdominal radiograph classically shows a hugely dilated loop arising from the pelvis, described as a coffee-bean or inverted-U sign pointing toward the right upper quadrant
In the absence of peritonitis or bowel compromise, initial treatment is endoscopic decompression (flexible sigmoidoscopy or rigid scope) with insertion of a flatus tube
Successful decompression relieves the acute episode but recurrence is common, so elective sigmoid resection is often advised in fit patients
Signs of peritonitis, failed decompression, or suspicion of gangrenous or perforated bowel mandate emergency laparotomy
At emergency operation for compromised bowel, resection (commonly a Hartmann's procedure) is performed rather than simple untwisting
A CT scan confirms the diagnosis, shows the whirl sign of the twisted mesentery, and assesses for ischaemia or perforation
reference.pathophysiology: Sigmoid volvulus occurs when a redundant, elongated sigmoid loop twists around its narrow mesenteric pedicle, producing a closed-loop large bowel obstruction. Chronic constipation and a lengthy, mobile sigmoid on a narrow mesenteric base predispose to torsion. The twist obstructs the lumen at both ends, and progressive distension raises intraluminal and intramural pressure. If the mesenteric vessels are compromised by the torsion, the loop becomes ischaemic, progressing to gangrene and perforation with faeculent peritonitis and sepsis. Massive gaseous distension of the closed loop is characteristic.
additionalDifferentials: Adhesional or hernia-related large bowel obstruction
additionalInvestigations: Plain abdominal radiograph for the characteristic dilated sigmoid loop
CT abdomen and pelvis to confirm the diagnosis, show the whirl sign, and assess for ischaemia or perforation
Bloods including full blood count, electrolytes, and lactate to gauge ischaemia and fitness for intervention
Endoscopic assessment of mucosal viability during attempted decompression
redFlags: Peritonitis, systemic sepsis, or shock suggesting ischaemic or perforated bowel (surgical emergency)
Bloodstained or necrotic mucosa or dark fluid at decompression indicating gangrene
Rising lactate, worsening distension, or free gas on imaging
reference.prognosis: Uncomplicated cases usually respond to endoscopic decompression but recur frequently unless definitive surgery is performed. Emergency surgery for gangrenous or perforated bowel in typically frail, elderly patients carries substantial morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Persisting with endoscopic decompression when peritonitis or ischaemia is present
Mistaking the presentation for simple constipation and delaying imaging
Failing to offer elective resection to fit patients after decompression, allowing recurrence
Overlooking an obstructing carcinoma as an alternative cause of distal large bowel obstruction
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Endoscopic decompression by flexible sigmoidoscopy or rigid scope with insertion of a flatus tube as first-line treatment in the absence of peritonitis or gangrene
Fluid resuscitation, correction of electrolyte disturbance and nasogastric decompression as supportive measures
Inspection of mucosal viability during endoscopy, abandoning decompression and proceeding to surgery if ischaemic mucosa is seen
Emergency laparotomy with resection, typically a Hartmann's procedure, for peritonitis, failed decompression or gangrenous or perforated bowel
Elective sigmoid resection after successful decompression in fit patients to prevent frequent recurrence
Monitoring for recurrence and for signs of bowel compromise following decompression
